blocks.cap: Gin's flat, the third drawer, the book he never showed you

blocks.p: The price sticker was still on the back. Three hundred and eighty yen, half peeled, curling up at one corner the way it must have curled for months every time Gin opened the drawer.

Third drawer. Under the charger. The voice on the voicemail had been almost nothing, almost Gin, and it had been right. Rei lifted out a cheap kraft-bound notebook, soft at the spine from being bent back, and held it as if it might be hot.

Rei sat on the floor beside the desk. The chair felt like it belonged to someone who was coming back, and he could not bear to presume. Outside the window the Obon lanterns were going up along the canal, small paper boxes of light meant to guide the dead home. They were not meant, he thought, for whatever was currently walking around in his brother.

He opened to the first page and the hand was Gin's. It was the cramped, leftward, apologetic hand Gin had had since he was nine, the one that always looked as if it were trying to take up less room than it had been given.

He read forward. The early entries were a tired man's entries. A closed case that closed too easily. A name in no file. The membrane over Kita-ku reading thin on instruments that should not have been able to read it at all. Gin was frightened in them, but it was an ordinary fright. It was the fright of a man who suspects he is right about something he would give anything to be wrong about.

In between the casework were the small lines Gin always wrote at the bottom of a page, the ones he signed off with. Rei had seen a hundred of them in the big Archive on the desk. Keys on the hook. Coffee terrible. Rei took the umbrella. Good. Here, in the cheap notebook, the small lines had begun to change.

doc.title: Gin's journal. Undated. Early.
lines: Coffee made before I remembered making it.
The apartment is starting to feel smaller than it used to. I do not think this is about the apartment.

blocks.p: Rei read that twice. He knew the coffee. He had come out of his room on more than one morning that summer and found a full pot already going cold, and Gin standing beside it looking faintly puzzled, as though the pot had made itself. Rei had laughed at him for it. He did not laugh now. A man who makes coffee without remembering he made it has lost a few minutes somewhere. Gin had noticed, and written it down, and gone on.

doc.title: Gin's journal. A Thursday.
lines: End of a long week. Something in the building across the street has been watching the window since Tuesday.
I have been noting it without addressing it, which is unlike me.
I have three theories. I am proceeding on the most comfortable one.

blocks.p: Rei got up and went to the window. The building across the street was a block of small flats with dark balconies and an air conditioner unit dripping on the third floor. Nothing looked back at him. He stood there until he felt foolish and then he stood there a little longer, because Gin had not been a man who felt watched for no reason.
A few pages later the watcher came back into the journal, and so did something worse.

doc.title: Gin's journal. Several days later.
lines: The thing across the street did not return after that first week. I have stopped noting its absence.
The thing across the street was not Rei. I have not fully resolved what it was. I have chosen not to pursue it further.
The reason. I am tired this week in a way that is not entirely accounted for by the caseload.

blocks.p: Was not Rei. Gin had checked whether the watching was his own brother. Rei understood that, and understood why. His own gift ran loud. Gin had told him so in a dozen careful ways over the years, and Rei had heard them as complaints about the mess in the kitchen. So Gin had looked at the pressure on the window and asked first whether it was only Rei, leaking through the wall. It was not. He had decided to let it go. He had been too tired to chase it.
Rei made himself keep reading.

blocks.break: The thing he thought was watching

blocks.p: Halfway through the notebook Gin had copied out a few lines from the classified part of the big Archive, the page he had captioned The thing the framework will not name. It described what the Directorate's research called the Architect Phenomenon. Not an entity, not a person, not a faction. An autonomous corrective mechanism, the veil's own slow response to a practitioner who hides a large rank for years without release. The outcomes listed were forced expression of the hidden power, sudden vulnerability to possession, disappearance, death, and now and then a strange survival in some new role. And the subject, the page said, usually knew. The Architect's attention felt like a specific quality of being watched.

doc.title: Gin's journal. Underneath.
lines: I have been aware of my status for approximately three years.

It is not threatening in the way an entity's attention is threatening. It is more like the feeling of a very large system becoming aware of a very small irregularity. Patient. Inevitable. Not personal.
I find this more frightening than I would find something personal. Personal things can be negotiated with. This cannot.
If you are a suppressor, if you have been masking your level, you should know that the math eventually balances. Not as threat. As information.

blocks.p: Rei knew what Gin was. Gin presented as a Ritualist, a C on the forms, and had presented as one for six years while holding something much larger underneath it. That was the Uedera habit. Stay sloppy. Stay unremarkable. Gin had taught it to Rei at the kitchen table before Rei could read. So when Gin began to feel watched by something huge and patient, he had reached for the only explanation his framework held. The veil itself had noticed what he was hiding, and was coming, slowly, to balance the books.

Rei sat on the floor with the notebook on his knees and felt the explanation wobble. He had read another page of Gin's that night, in the chapter on demons, and a single line of it would not leave him alone. Demons produce directional membrane thinning around their location. The thinning points toward rather than radiating from. The Architect, Gin had written, was a system. It was not personal. But the thing across the street had not watched the whole district. It had watched one window.
He did not know yet. He put a pencil mark beside the Architect page and went on.

Near the middle there was a folder note, copied across from the big Archive, with a small piece of tape stuck to its corner. Gin had always taped the folders he did not trust, to see if anyone opened them.

doc.title: Observation Log 7-C. Kita thin spot
lines: Three anchor signatures in a pattern around the Kita thin spot. I have been documenting them for eight months.
I put a small piece of tape on the folder and checked.
Rei has walked past the thin spot twelve times in the last month. I've counted. I'm counting.

doc.title: CVD Research Division. Veil Stability Mapping Project. Phase III. Protocol Eyes Only
lines: Veil Stability Anchor Signatures. Open research question.

Phase III identified anomalous stability signatures globally, points where the membrane is reinforced rather than thinned, in ways no geographic or practitioner-density model predicts. The report calls them self-organizing reinforcement nodes. The practitioners who work near them call them the warm spots.
The signatures correlate with specific emotional registers in surrounding human and entity populations. They have been continuously active for longer than the project's historical data reaches.
Practitioners operating in the influence radius of an anchor signature show subtle stability variations the standard mapping does not predict. Mechanism unconfirmed.

blocks.p: Gin's caption under the Phase III page said only The same room. Very different weather. Three warm spots around one cold wound, and his little brother walking past the wound twelve times a month without knowing it was there. Rei had walked that way to the konbini. He had walked it because it was quicker.
Then he reached the entry dated the fourteenth of August. It was three lines long and it ended mid-sentence.

doc.title: Gin's journal. 14 August.
lines: Long shift. Walked home alone, late, the dense way along the canal, because I could not face the train.
Rei's light was on under his door when I got in. Did not eat. Did not knock.
I need to sleep before I

blocks.p: The next page was dated the same night, an hour later. The handwriting had changed.

Not wildly. That was the part that got into him and stayed. It had only become a little more even. A little more upright. As though someone had studied Gin's hand for an afternoon and then, being a careful student, written it back to Rei slightly improved.

Rei sat with that for a long time while the lantern light moved on the wall. He understood that he was looking at the exact hour. It was not a metaphor for it and not a memory of it. It was the seam itself, two pages, one man on either side. His hands were cold. He wanted very badly to close the book and decide it was grief making patterns.
But he had read enough of Gin's casework to know that the impulse to un-see a thing is the impulse the thing is counting on. So he turned the page, into the entries the new hand had written.

blocks.cap: The order it wants you to read in, and the place your own thoughts go

blocks.p: The numbers in the margins were small and untroubled, the way a librarian's are. If he followed them, the journal stopped being a record and became an argument, beautifully shelved. Here was the grief of 2011 that had never been given its rite. Beside it, the membrane that had been weeping ever since. Beside that, the single seat at the Thirteen's table that had stood vacant long enough for the weeping to have a remedy, if only someone with the right grade and the right wound would consent to feel the obligation.

None of it was a lie. That was what he kept having to put the book down over. Each entry was a true thing, and the order stacked the true things at an angle. Somewhere around the ninth page Rei caught himself nodding. The nod was the cost.

He had thought he would be fighting something. He was only listening, and listening leaves marks. He learned to feel the seam by the temperature of the wanting under each line. Gin's entries, the ones in the older leftward hand, grew fewer every page. They wanted him to stop. They were clumsy and they repeated themselves and they said go home in four different broken ways. They were unmistakably the writing of a man trying to shout through a wall while someone held his hand.

The other entries were calmer, and they wanted him closer. They wanted him to understand. They reasoned with him the way a person reasons with a frightened animal they intend to keep. The worst of it was how good the reasoning was. On a clearer night he would nearly have signed his name under it.

An hour in, he noticed that he had begun to think in its cadence. When he reached for his own objection, it arrived already softened, already shelved in the new hand's order, already wearing the little marginal number it would have had if the new hand had written it. His body called it a kind of seasickness. The floor of his own mind was tilting a few degrees toward a frame that was not his.

Gin had a word for that. Gin had a whole chapter for it, the one he had left open on the kitchen table twice. Both times Rei had closed it without reading it. He reached up now, pulled the big Archive down off the desk, and found the chapter. On its first page, in Gin's margin, were three lines.

doc.title: Chapter Five. Gin's margin note
lines: Three readings. Never confuse them.
Health is the body, and only the body takes it. A blow, a fall, a ridden host's hands.
Stability is the anchor that holds you closed against the veil. It is what power and dread spend, and what the dead lean on. As it falls the membrane opens. At zero you are wide open.
Madness is the slow corruption pooling. It climbs when the veil gets in, above all through broken Stability, and it does not wash out.
A practitioner ends one of two ways and they are not the same death. The body fails. Or the self does. The anchor breaks, Madness fills, and something else moves into the empty room.
Rank and Stability are two separate axes. Rank is what you can do. Stability is whether doing it ends you.

blocks.p: So that was the tilt. It was not madness, not yet. It was Stability, spending itself on every page he turned.

His hand was already closing the journal. He watched it do that, the way a person watches their own foot step back from the edge of a platform. It would be so easy to stop. He would sleep. He would wake up knowing less, and feeling better, and his brother would still be a smooth voice on the phone.
He thought of Gin at this same desk, writing a chapter he knew Rei would close twice without reading. Writing it anyway.
Rei opened the journal again at the page he had left.

blocks.cap: The tell, near the back, where the warmth points the wrong way

blocks.p: In the end it was not a horror that gave it away. It was a kindness.

Near the back, in the even upright hand, there was an entry about Rei. It was warm. It remembered the summer Rei broke his wrist and how Gin had carried his bag for a month. It used the small name only Gin used. Rei was reading it with his throat tight, almost grateful, when the seasickness saved him.

He had read this exact warmth before, in Gin's casework, forty pages earlier in the old leftward hand. It was the section Gin had written about telling a worn host from a whole one. Rei turned back and found it.

doc.title: Gin's journal. Casework. The old hand.
lines: What it cannot calibrate is the direction of the warmth. It orients toward whoever is currently useful, rather than toward whoever the host actually cared about.
This is the tell. It has saved my life twice and I am not being dramatic about that.
The tell is never the warmth itself. It is the direction the warmth points. A demon keeps the host's whole register of affection and aims all of it at whoever is useful now.

blocks.p: Read it backward and the entry about the broken wrist was not love remembering him. It was love being aimed.

He understood, then, what class of feeling he had been swimming in for three hours. He understood why it worked on him in particular. It was Gin's warmth, accurate to the gram, pointed at Rei because Rei was the hands it wanted. The older entries never aimed. They blundered toward him, repetitive and useless, asking nothing, wanting only that he live.

That was how he would tell them apart from now on, in every text and every lucid window and every reasonable favour still to come. Not by the wrongness, which it could sand away. By the direction of the wanting. Gin wanted him safe and gone. The thing wanted him near and helpful. The voice that wanted something from him was never the one that loved him, however perfectly it had learned to sound as if it did.

Rei closed the journal. The lantern light was all the way up the wall now. Across the canal the paper boxes were drifting out onto the black water, each one a small consent to let the dead be guided home. He was not going to get to do that for Gin tonight, or maybe ever. The cost of the last three hours sat in him like cold water at the base of the spine. He could feel, distinctly, the few degrees his own floor had not returned to level.
But he knew the seam now. He could hear it. Knowing where a thing ended and his brother began was the first tool he had been handed that the thing could not take back by being reasonable.
He set the journal on the desk beside the big Archive and looked at the two of them together, and something about the picture bothered him.

A neighbour had seen a man wearing Gin's face fit a key to this door. Whoever that was had stood in this room, at this desk, while Rei was out. He had left the lamp on. He had left the Archive open, six months of Gin's writing about exactly what he was. And he had left the journal in its drawer, with the seam in it and the warmth that pointed the wrong way, for anyone to find.

A careful thing does not leave evidence lying on a desk. Rei could not think why it would. He wrote the question on the inside cover of the journal in pencil, small, so he would not forget it. Why didn't it burn these?
Then he pulled the lamp down to the floor, opened the Archive at the chapter Gin had told him to read twice, and began.
